question: Which cold calls produced a follow-up, and what did the successful ones have in common?

resolution.read_instruction: Extract every explicit next step agreed or proposed at the end of the call (follow-up meeting, demo, trial, email, proposal, call back), whether it was accepted, declined, or left open, and the stated reason or interest level of the prospect. Also extract what OrbitFlow staff said or did that led to the outcome, including the pitch used, the problem discussed, the role of the contact, and any objections raised and how they were handled.
assumptions: Cold call question interpreted as covering calls CALL-016 to CALL-020 only.
'Successful' is not defined; treated as calls where a follow-up was agreed, so the reader should capture the outcome and the reasons so success can be compared afterwards.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: I'll send one email in February with something specific about Power Automate and where it does and doesn't hold up in manufacturing. If it's useful, reply.
findings.context: Vendor proposed a single follow-up email in February instead of further calls, and the prospect accepted it. — Explicit next step agreed at end of call; it is an email, not a meeting, demo, or trial, and the prospect agreed only to one email.

findings.speaker: Dermot Kelly
findings.quote: February's fine. One email.
findings.context: Prospect accepted the February email but with a clear limit: one email only. — Acceptance is conditional and low-commitment; prospect said it was fine, not that he wanted a meeting.

findings.speaker: Dermot Kelly
findings.quote: It's a "we finished an ERP migration in March and I've told everyone in this building that nobody is buying any new software this year."
findings.context: Prospect declined engagement this year because of a recent ERP migration and a company-wide freeze on new software purchases. — Stated reason for low interest; timing objection rather than a product objection.

findings.speaker: Dermot Kelly
findings.quote: we've got Power Automate through our Microsoft deal, so it'd have to be pretty compelling.
findings.context: Prospect said the company already has Power Automate via its Microsoft deal, so any alternative would need to be compelling. — Objection about existing tooling; vendor acknowledged it as common among Microsoft shops and did not argue the point.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: The specific thing we usually fix is that nobody can see where something's stuck until it's late.
findings.context: Vendor's pitch centred on operations teams in manufacturing where handoffs happen over email and spreadsheets and stuck work is only visible late. — Opening pitch; prospect said it 'lands' but still declined to look at anything.

findings.speaker: Dermot Kelly
findings.quote: It'd be me and it'd be our IT director jointly.
findings.context: Prospect is not the sole owner of the workflow layer; he would share ownership with the IT director, which is the contact role relevant to any future decision. — Vendor asked who would own the workflow layer after the ERP project; the answer defines the buying group.

findings.speaker: Dermot Kelly
findings.quote: You're the fourth this month.
findings.context: Prospect's interest level is low; the call ended with no meeting, demo, or call-back scheduled, and the outcome is inferred as unlikely to convert soon. — Inferred from tone and repeated refusals; vendor agreed not to call again this year.

findings.speaker: Martine Duval
findings.quote: Send me the page and copy Chloe. If the page is good she'll put it in the diary.
findings.context: Martine Duval agreed to a follow-up: she asked for a one-page document to be sent, with Chloe copied, and said that if the page is good Chloe would put a meeting in the diary. The meeting itself was not confirmed. — Outcome of the cold call; the follow-up is conditional on the page being good and was left open rather than a meeting being booked.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: One page. And can I ask for thirty minutes in the week of the sixth? Not a demo. I'd want to understand the disruption process before I show you anything.
findings.context: Leo Grant proposed a one-page follow-up and a 30-minute meeting in the week of the sixth, explicitly not a demo, to understand the disruption process first. — Next step proposed by the vendor; the meeting was not confirmed on the call.

findings.speaker: Martine Duval
findings.quote: Not a deck. Something short that describes what you'd actually look at.
findings.context: Martine asked for something short describing what OrbitFlow would actually look at, not a deck. — Prospect's stated preference for the follow-up format.

findings.speaker: Chloe Barnes
findings.quote: Honestly? Probably. Thursday or Friday.
findings.context: The call got through because the contact (Chloe, executive assistant) was persuaded to put Leo through; Chloe had earlier said a call back on Thursday or Friday was better, then offered to check whether Martine was free after her previous call. — Initial call was a gatekeeper screen; the vendor's candour about not being expected and the 'what makes her engage' question led to the transfer.

findings.speaker: Chloe Barnes
findings.quote: She responds to specifics. If you say "workflow automation" she'll be polite for a minute and then get off. If you say something about our actual business she'll listen.
findings.context: Chloe advised that Martine responds to specifics about the business rather than generic 'workflow automation' talk. — Gatekeeper's advice on what engages the decision-maker; the vendor then opened with a travel-specific disruption scenario.

findings.speaker: Martine Duval
findings.quote: It's handled badly. It's handled by a very good team working very hard, which is not the same as handled.
findings.context: Leo's pitch used a travel disruption scenario (flight cancellation involving rebooking, supplier notification, customer communication, refund/credit across four systems), which Martine confirmed as accurate. She said the process is handled, but 'badly', relying on a very good team working very hard. — Problem discussed that engaged the prospect; the vendor deferred the deeper discussion because of time pressure.

findings.speaker: Martine Duval
findings.quote: She said three.
findings.context: Martine's interest appeared moderate and time-limited: she gave only about five minutes and kept referring to the clock, but she engaged with the disruption problem and invited follow-up material. — Inferred from tone; the call was short and constrained by her schedule and a supplier conference.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: Half an hour, in the next couple of weeks, with you and whoever owns the housing management system technically.
findings.context: A follow-up meeting was agreed: a half-hour call in the next couple of weeks (week of the sixth) with Ade and the owner of the housing management system, with no demo. — Explicit next step agreed at end of call; Maya proposed a discovery-style call, Ade accepted and said he would get Priya.

findings.speaker: Ade Balogun
findings.quote: Alright. Send me the technical requirements, I'll send you the frameworks, and I'll get Priya. Week of the sixth?
findings.context: Ade accepted the follow-up and set a date, while Maya committed to checking framework coverage and sending technical requirements. — Prospect acceptance of next step; vendor homework before meeting.

findings.speaker: Ade Balogun
findings.quote: It was a much better cold call than I expected too.
findings.context: Ade's interest was high: he said the call was going better than expected and that the discovery approach was sensible. — Prospect sentiment toward the vendor's approach, which included declining to pitch a demo.

findings.speaker: Ade Balogun
findings.quote: That's most of my job, actually.
findings.context: The pitch framed the problem as cross-team processes with no owner, where work sits and is found out late. Ade matched it to his voids (empty property turnaround) process, which he said was most of his job. — Problem discussed led to engagement; the contact was head of business change who owned the problem.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: The first phase of something like this shouldn't be automating the voids process. It should be instrumenting it.
findings.context: Vendor declined to pitch a demo and proposed instrumenting the voids process first (timestamps only, eight weeks) rather than automating, which the prospect found appealing. — Vendor objection handling that reduced scope; prospect said it would be considerably cheaper.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: I'd want to know which frameworks you use and whether we're on any of them
findings.context: Vendor raised procurement and integration risks up front. Ade said most vendors discover procurement late, and he noted the lack of connectors for his sector. — Objections raised by vendor and acknowledged by prospect; prospect did not object to continuing.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: I'll be honest — I don't have a housing association reference.
findings.context: Vendor admitted no housing association references; Ade said this was a procurement problem, not his, but asked that it be raised with Priya. — Negative fact disclosed by vendor; prospect deferred it.

findings.speaker: Ade Balogun
findings.quote: If I ask her. She's sceptical of vendors, which I'd say is a feature.
findings.context: Prospect's technical contact Priya Menon (applications manager) was identified as the second attendee; Ade said she was sceptical of vendors and would likely attend. — Role of the contact; the follow-up depends on Ade getting her to attend.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: if we're not on any of them I'll tell you and we can decide whether it's worth continuing.
findings.context: Vendor said that if the framework check fails, they would tell Ade and decide whether to continue. — Conditional next step; Ade received it without objection.

findings.speaker: Yvonne Deeks
findings.quote: You can send it. I'll be honest with you, I won't read it.
findings.context: Prospect agreed to receive information from OrbitFlow but said she would not read it, so the only proposed next step was an email with no expected engagement. — Vendor proposed sending information at end of call; prospect accepted with an explicit caveat. Outcome left open with low interest.

findings.speaker: Yvonne Deeks
findings.quote: I'd rather tell you that than have you follow up four times.
findings.context: Prospect declined repeated follow-up contact and preferred a direct no over being chased. — Explains why she accepted the send-info offer only nominally; reason for refusing further follow-up.

findings.speaker: Yvonne Deeks
findings.quote: For something like this? Two, three hundred a month, and I'd have to justify it.
findings.context: Prospect's stated objection was price: she could justify only about two to three hundred a month against an OrbitFlow entry package starting at eighteen hundred a month. — Vendor quoted £1,800/month entry package for up to thirty users (T026); prospect raised budget objection repeatedly.

findings.speaker: Yvonne Deeks
findings.quote: You're not it.
findings.context: Prospect's final outcome was a clear rejection: OrbitFlow is not a fit for her group. — Vendor concluded the call as a no-fit; no meeting, demo, or trial was booked.

findings.speaker: Yvonne Deeks
findings.quote: You don't actually know anything about us, do you.
findings.context: Prospect said the vendor did not know anything about her group and had only read basic public information, which was the main reason for her disengagement. — Prospect cited the generic pitch and misstated referral flow (outbound not inbound) as evidence the vendor had not researched the group.

findings.speaker: Alastair McCrae
findings.quote: So what we'd typically do is come in, look at your onboarding processes, your compliance, your referrals, and just automate the whole lot.
findings.context: OrbitFlow's opening pitch was generic, applying a template of onboarding, compliance and referral automation without knowing the prospect's operations. — Vendor pitch made before any discovery questions; prospect later corrected the referral assumption.

findings.speaker: Yvonne Deeks
findings.quote: It's not a process problem, it's that nobody wants to be a dental nurse for what we can afford to pay.
findings.context: Prospect's biggest challenge is dental nurse recruitment, which she said is not a process problem that OrbitFlow could fix. — Vendor tied the recruitment pain to onboarding automation; prospect rejected that link, citing pay as the real cause.

findings.speaker: Yvonne Deeks
findings.quote: He fixes printers.
findings.context: When asked about another contact for a follow-up, the prospect offered only a part-time person who fixes printers, so no alternate decision-maker was identified. — Vendor asked whether an IT person should be spoken to; prospect's answer dismissed the lead.

findings.speaker: Rafael Santos
findings.quote: Send me something short — not a deck — on how you'd approach the seven-stage thing, and specifically on the operations-can-change-it question.
findings.context: Prospect agreed to receive a short written note from OrbitFlow on the seven-stage approach and the operations-can-change-it question, and said he would do a thirty-minute call if the note was good; the follow-up is conditional and left open. — Explicit next step at end of cold call; accepted conditionally, not a booked meeting. Note was requested by the prospect, not pitched by vendor.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: Would it be worth a thirty-minute call before mid-October? Not a pitch.
findings.context: Vendor proposed a thirty-minute call before mid-October, framed as non-pitch, to walk through structuring the seven stages; prospect asked whether it was worth it given they would probably pick Tray, then said 'Send the note. If it's good I'll do the thirty minutes.' — Vendor's follow-up proposal; prospect deferred acceptance pending the note. Vendor noted the prospect would likely choose a competitor.

findings.speaker: Rafael Santos
findings.quote: Your website. It's very enterprise. Governance, compliance, workspace separation. We're a hundred and fifty people building robots.
findings.context: Prospect had crossed OrbitFlow off his list about a month before because the website looked too enterprise (governance, compliance, workspace separation) for a 150-person robotics firm; vendor agreed the marketing targets companies with a governance function. — Initial objection to the vendor; the vendor conceded the website fit rather than arguing, which the prospect remarked on.

findings.speaker: Rafael Santos
findings.quote: Tray don't have a connector and we're looking at building against its API, which our one back-end developer estimates at three weeks.
findings.context: Prospect's reason for engaging at all was an ERP integration gap in the ongoing Tray.io evaluation (no connector, API build estimated at three weeks, prospect thinks six); vendor said it likely lacks a native connector either and offered no advantage on that point. — Vendor conceded the point rather than pitching; prospect is three weeks into a Tray.io evaluation with a decision around 14 October.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: Run it against Tray — I mean that, run it against Tray, you're three weeks in and it costs you nothing.
findings.context: Vendor declined to pitch against the incumbent evaluation, advising a third vendor three weeks in was wasteful, and instead proposed a one-week test for operations staff to change workflows without the developer; prospect said they would not restart the evaluation. — Vendor steered away from a demo and toward a test that favours Tray; prospect's interest is real but limited.

findings.speaker: Rafael Santos
findings.quote: Mid-October. Fourteenth, I think, or thereabouts.
findings.context: Prospect stated decision timing: mid-October, around the 14th, and would not move the decision date. — Constrains any follow-up window; the vendor's proposed call must happen before this.

findings.speaker: Rafael Santos
findings.quote: a month is a month of revenue on a two hundred thousand pound order.
findings.context: Prospect values the outcome at roughly a month of revenue per two-hundred-thousand-pound order with eleven orders in flight, which he framed as board-level material; vendor used this to frame the value of instrumenting the stages. — Vendor's value argument for follow-up; prospect's interest in the topic is stated, not a purchase commitment.

draft.answer: Four of the five cold calls ended with some follow-up agreed, but only Beacon Housing Trust produced a firm, dated meeting [C1]. Silverline Travel and Kestrel Robotics agreed to a short written note with a meeting conditional on its quality [C2][C3]. Quarry Ridge Foods agreed only to one email [C4], and Trafford Dental Group effectively rejected OrbitFlow [C5]. The calls that went furthest shared a problem-specific pitch and a no-demo, discovery-style ask [C6].

claims.text: Beacon Housing Trust (CALL-018) was the strongest result: Ade Balogun accepted a half-hour no-demo call in the week of the sixth with the owner of the housing management system (Priya Menon, applications manager, who is sceptical of vendors and whom Ade would ask to attend). Maya Chen was to check framework coverage and send technical requirements, and Ade would send the frameworks. If the vendor is on none of the frameworks, Maya said she would tell him and they would decide whether to continue.

Silverline Travel (CALL-017): Martine Duval asked Leo Grant for a short one-page document, not a deck, with Chloe Barnes copied. If the page is good, Chloe would put a meeting in the diary. Leo had proposed 30 minutes in the week of the sixth, but no meeting was confirmed.

Kestrel Robotics (CALL-020): COO Rafael Santos asked for a short note, not a deck, on the seven-stage approach and the operations-can-change-it question, and said he would do a thirty-minute call if the note was good. The follow-up is conditional and unbooked. His decision is around 14 October, and he is evaluating Tray.io and would not restart the evaluation.

Quarry Ridge Foods (CALL-016): Dermot Kelly accepted only one email from Maya Chen in February, with no meeting. He cited an ERP migration, a freeze on software purchases, and existing Power Automate. His interest appears low, and the vendor agreed not to call again this year.

Trafford Dental Group (CALL-019): Yvonne Deeks said OrbitFlow could send information but she would not read it, and she rejected further follow-up. Her reasons were price (£1,800/month against her roughly £200-300 budget) and a generic pitch from Alastair McCrae. She ended with 'You're not it', with no meeting booked.

Common factors in the stronger outcomes: the pitch was tied to the prospect's own problem. Ade matched the pitch to his voids process, and Martine confirmed the flight-disruption scenario was handled badly. Vendors also avoided a demo and proposed low-commitment discovery or a note. In Beacon's case the vendor was candid about gaps, and in Kestrel's it conceded the Tray.io integration point. Trafford's generic pitch, by contrast, led to disengagement.

not_covered: Whether any of the follow-ups actually took place after the calls.
Any cold calls outside CALL-016 to CALL-020.
assumptions: Only CALL-016 to CALL-020 were treated as cold calls.
'Successful' means a follow-up was agreed; the commonalities are inferred by comparing the findings across calls.

evidence.context: Vendor raised procurement and integration risks up front. Ade said most vendors discover procurement late, and he noted the lack of connectors for his sector. — Objections raised by vendor and acknowledged by prospect; prospect did not object to continuing.

evidence.context: Prospect's reason for engaging at all was an ERP integration gap in the ongoing Tray.io evaluation (no connector, API build estimated at three weeks, prospect thinks six); vendor said it likely lacks a native connector either and offered no advantage on that point. — Vendor conceded the point rather than pitching; prospect is three weeks into a Tray.io evaluation with a decision around 14 October.

evidence.speaker: Leo Grant
evidence.quote: Run it against Tray — I mean that, run it against Tray, you're three weeks in and it costs you nothing.
evidence.context: Vendor declined to pitch against the incumbent evaluation, advising a third vendor three weeks in was wasteful, and instead proposed a one-week test for operations staff to change workflows without the developer; prospect said they would not restart the evaluation. — Vendor steered away from a demo and toward a test that favours Tray; prospect's interest is real but limited.

evidence.quote: So what we'd typically do is come in, look at your onboarding processes, your compliance, your referrals, and just automate the whole lot.
evidence.context: OrbitFlow's opening pitch was generic, applying a template of onboarding, compliance and referral automation without knowing the prospect's operations. — Vendor pitch made before any discovery questions; prospect later corrected the referral assumption.

evidence.quote: You don't actually know anything about us, do you.
evidence.context: Prospect said the vendor did not know anything about her group and had only read basic public information, which was the main reason for her disengagement. — Prospect cited the generic pitch and misstated referral flow (outbound not inbound) as evidence the vendor had not researched the group.
